title: Migrating Java Code to Kotlin
learning_outcomes: Explain the central rule or purpose of migrating java code to kotlin using at least one correct term from the lesson.
Interpret or adapt a small Kotlin example that demonstrates migrating java code to kotlin.
Identify one relevant edge case, debugging step, or version/platform constraint.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn **Migrating Java Code to Kotlin** as part of **Kotlin and Java Interoperability**. Kotlin and Java interoperate, but platform types, annotations, generated JVM signatures, and collection mutability require explicit boundary checks. Use the subtopics—Automatic Conversion and Its Limits, Improving Converted Code, Interoperability Testing—as a checklist: predict what the example will do, then verify it in a project configured for the target platform.
content.why_it_matters: Real projects depend on reliable error handling, modular organization, reproducible builds, and safe language boundaries. This lesson helps turn isolated syntax into maintainable applications.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Kotlin and Java interoperate, but platform types, annotations, generated JVM signatures, and collection mutability require explicit boundary checks.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with automatic conversion and its limits. Then compare it with improving converted code. Identify the input, state, dependency, or branch that determines the result. The snippet is a static reference for CodeLeaf and is not executed in the lesson page.

items.title: Automatic Conversion and Its Limits
items.text: Automatic Conversion and Its Limits means checking the boundary between the language feature and its compiler, runtime, plugin, library, or target version. Pin the versions used by the project and verify documented support before depending on the behavior.

items.title: Improving Converted Code
items.text: Improving Converted Code is one part of migrating java code to kotlin. Connect its definition to the example, identify the input/state it changes, and verify the expected behavior with a small test case.

items.title: Interoperability Testing
items.text: Interoperability Testing means checking the boundary between the language feature and its compiler, runtime, plugin, library, or target version. Pin the versions used by the project and verify documented support before depending on the behavior.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Save the snippet in a Kotlin/JVM console project and run the configured Gradle application task, or use the Kotlin Playground for examples that need no external dependencies.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the documented starting values, rerun the smallest test, and compare the result with the expected output. If behavior differs, check the compiler/plugin/runtime versions and the active target before changing more than one thing.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake to avoid
content_blocks.text: Migrating Java Code to Kotlin removes the need to test boundary conditions or verify the chosen runtime/library version.

content_blocks.title: Troubleshooting and reset
content_blocks.text: If the example fails, first confirm which runtime/project type the snippet requires. Read the first useful compiler or runtime message, check imports and declared dependencies, reduce the example to a minimal case, and rerun. For target-specific code, use the target toolchain rather than assuming a console or browser runner can execute it.

items.title: Verify

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small variation that demonstrates migrating java code to kotlin. Write down your predicted result first, run it in the correct local project, then explain one boundary case involving automatic conversion and its limits.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain migrating java code to kotlin without copying the lesson wording.
